I didn't look up the NAS-Bench-201 tables. These numbers are estimates from how the cell is structured: which edges sit on the same path, and when an edit makes an edge irrelevant.

- **Disconnection cases (low numbers).** When the condition already weakens a path, removing another edge on the remaining paths hurts more. That makes the effect LOWER, so claims 0, 2, 9, 11 and 24 get low numbers.
- **Irrelevance cases (low numbers).** If the condition makes the edited edge irrelevant, the edit's effect drops to about zero. That is below its usual positive effect for a conv. This applies to 19 (edge 0 is none, so node 1 is dead) and 20 (edge 5 is none, so node 2 never reaches the output).
- **Replacement cases (higher numbers).** When the condition is about which op gets replaced, swapping out a weak op gains more than the average swap. This applies to 5 and 10 (replacing avg_pool) and 21 (replacing none).
- **Everything else** is close to 50, because I had no strong structural reason to lean either way.
